narrative:
The model predicted a 67% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your class ranking in the third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your undergraduate GPA. Your third-year ranking had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. While the average accepted student ranked around the middle of their class (decile 5.8), you placed in the second decile, a noticeably weaker academic position. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure; at 26 it sits well below the 37-point average of students who were admitted. These two elements together created a clear signal of higher risk.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.5 worked in the opposite direction. It is higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore nudged the prediction slightly toward success. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not large enough to overcome the combined impact of your class rank and LSAT.

The school’s decision was driven entirely by these academic performance indicators; neither your gender, race, nor family income (which falls in the middle bracket) played any role.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class standing in the remaining law school years and consider retaking the LSAT to bring your score closer to the typical range of admitted students. Stronger results in either area could meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor. (248 words)
